newsitem.title: UK: Who's afraid of EMU delay? Not the French markets.
newsitem.headline: Who's afraid of EMU delay? Not the French markets.

text.p: Not many French financial traders and analysts seem willing to bet that the January 1, 1999 start date for European economic and monetary union (EMU) will be postponed, even if they might think it.
France's financial markets have barely flinched during a rumour-strewn couple of weeks, financial analysts said on Tuesday.

Currencies of countries on the European periphery, like the Italian lira, Spanish peseta and Swedish crown, have come under growing pressure in recent weeks as investors reassess their prospects of starting monetary union on time in 1999.
But the extent to which this concern has suddenly mushroomed into fears of a delay to the whole EMU project is still unclear.

Judging by the lack of reaction in French markets to this recent wave of EMU scepticism, either people are not willing to bet against a generalised EMU delay or they think French bond and currency prices would not react to a postponement.

"I think you have to look at the mark/Paris exchange rate and the stability we've seen there is a clear indication that we do not yet have an EMU crisis on our hands," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago.
"Talk about eventual delay is understandable but the timing is all wrong. Politicians have neither the need nor desire to deal with the delay option for at least another year."
Delay talk is fuelled by concern that record unemployment could mean Germany itself may miss a narrow reading of the budget deficit targets necessary for EMU.

Yet, the letter of the Maastricht Treaty allows for cyclical downturns as well as the budget deficits being "close" to three percent of gross domestic product. How this is read unlikely to be decided until the first candidates for EMU are chosen early next year, analysts said.
None of the current speculation and rumour seems confident enough yet to disturb the core of the EMU bloc.
